{{short description|For 3 circles, the intersection of the radical axes of each pair}}
{{Use American English|date=November 2020}}
[[File:Radical center.svg|thumb|right|250px|
'''Diagram of the radical center of three circles.'''
{{legend-line|solid #222222 2px|Given circles}}
{{legend-line|solid blue 2px|Radical axis of each pair of given circles}}
{{legend|#9c5f5a|Radical center (intersection of the radical axes)}}
{{legend-line|solid orange 2px|Radical circle (intersects the given circles [[Orthogonal circles|orthogonally]])}}]]

In [[geometry]], the '''power center''' of three [[circle]]s, also called the '''radical center''',  is the [[Intersection (geometry)|intersection point]] of the three [[radical axis|radical axes]] of the pairs of circles.  If the radical center lies outside of all three circles, then it is the center of the unique circle (the '''radical circle''') that intersects the three given circles [[orthogonal circles|orthogonally]]; the construction of this orthogonal circle corresponds to '''Monge's problem'''.  This is a special case of the [https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ThreeConicsTheorem.html three conics theorem].

The three radical axes meet in a single point, the radical center, for the following reason.  The radical axis of a pair of circles is defined as the set of points that have equal [[power of a point|power]] {{mvar|h}} with respect to both circles.  For example, for every point {{mvar|P}} on the radical axis of circles 1 and 2, the powers to each circle are equal: {{math|1=''h''<sub>1</sub> = ''h''<sub>2</sub>}}.  Similarly, for every point on the radical axis of circles 2 and 3, the powers must be equal, {{math|1=''h''<sub>2</sub> = ''h''<sub>3</sub>}}.  Therefore, at the [[Line–line intersection|intersection point of these two lines]], all three powers must be equal, {{math|1=''h''<sub>1</sub> = ''h''<sub>2</sub> = ''h''<sub>3</sub>}}.  Since [[Equality (mathematics)#Basic properties|this implies]] that {{math|1=''h''<sub>1</sub> = ''h''<sub>3</sub>}}, this point must also lie on the radical axis of circles 1 and 3.  Hence, all three radical axes pass through the same point, the radical center.

The radical center has several applications in geometry. It has an important role in a solution to [[problem of Apollonius|Apollonius' problem]] published by [[Joseph Diaz Gergonne]] in 1814. In the [[power diagram]] of a system of circles, all of the vertices of the diagram are located at radical centers of triples of circles. The [[Spieker center]] of a [[triangle]] is the radical center of its [[excircles]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Some triangle centers associated with the circles tangent to the excircles|journal=Forum Geometricorum|url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2010volume10/FG201006.pdf|volume=10|year=2010|pages=35–40|first=Boris|last=Odenhal}}</ref>  Several types of radical circles have been defined as well, such as the radical circle of the [[Lucas circle]]s.
